beats.trigger: ## Security
beats.got: nothing new; a module title.

beats.trigger: The key is to find the approach that works for your organisation and to keep iterating as the landscape changes.
beats.got: The first sentence says to run a check instead of waiting for certainty. The paragraph after it is boilerplate I've read in every vendor deck.

beats.trigger: The Module 4 prework adds two reads: (1) personal skills as the package format that carries expertise into your agent, (2) agent risk layered on top of normal security work.
beats.got: There are three or four reading links, and I'd skim them before the session.

beats.trigger: **Distinguish** compliant / violating / "I can't tell" for each rule
beats.got: The list is long and jargon-heavy. The compliant / violating / "I can't tell" triage is the useful part.

beats.trigger: Name the thing you'd want to check before letting this near a real stakeholder.
beats.got: It asks me to pick the thing I'd want to check before this goes near my pricing working group. That's a real question and I'd answer it.

beats.trigger: A tool call is not a new species of work. It is text crossing a boundary into action.
beats.got: A tool call is just text that the runtime turns into an action. That's a decent mental model, but it's more mechanism than I need.

beats.trigger: Would you bet your job on it being safe?
beats.got: The opening hook lands. The paragraph about analysts and "capture the benefits of AI" is filler, and I stopped reading it.

beats.trigger: Your firewall doesn't see it because your firewall has never had to worry about persuasion.
beats.got: The attack comes as ordinary English in a document the agent reads, so the old perimeter thinking doesn't apply. I hadn't thought of my churn article that way.

beats.trigger: Scope (give the agent less). Split (break it into two agents with different trust levels). Filter (post-process the output before it leaves). Gate (a human approves before a sensitive action). Review (a second agent judges the first's output).
beats.got: There are five concrete mitigation moves. I can map each to something I'd tell my team.

beats.trigger: Accept the residual on record, or close the door.
beats.got: Write down the residual risk and then either accept it or close the door. This is the same thing my CFO would ask me.

beats.trigger: You can't buy certainty. You can run a loop.
beats.got: It's the same point as before, said more dramatically, so nothing new. The "Damn, this is complex stuff" line felt out of place.

beats.trigger: A **skill** packages an expertise (rules, checklists, the moves an agent runs) into something the agent can load and use.
beats.got: A skill is a reusable bundle of how-to that the agent loads. That's closer to what my team of fourteen needs than another prompt.

beats.trigger: The raw run shows which rules can be checked from files and which ones need judgment, context, or a standing evidence check.
beats.got: Running the policy files against my system shows which rules a file check can settle and which need a human.

beats.trigger: The reusable check is supposed to carry what matters in your system, not generic GDPR.
beats.got: I tell the agent in my own words what matters, such as pricing data and the customer names the CEO wouldn't want in a transcript, and the check gets built around that.

beats.trigger: You'll get a lot of questions. The grill is wide on purpose: the agent probes both lenses and won't stop at one round.
beats.got: The agent will interview me at length to build the policy lens and the agent-risk lens. It's long, but I can see where it goes.

beats.trigger: hand the rest back: *"You choose. Optimise for what I can't steer."*
beats.got: I answer what I know and delegate the rest, then check that all four risk patterns are in the package.

beats.trigger: The save mechanic differs by runtime.
beats.got: The saving steps differ across runtimes. I only need the one I use, and my team would need to be told which.

beats.trigger: The policy files are source material. The reusable check is the expert in the room.
beats.got: The valuable thing isn't the policy files or a clever prompt. It's the packaged check that carries judgment and can be rerun.

beats.trigger: The goal is not a clean bill of health.
beats.got: The goal is to run the assess, mitigate, reassess loop once on my real system. That sets the right expectation.

beats.trigger: Type `/` in the prompt and look for `/security-audit` in the autocomplete list.
beats.got: I type a slash and check that the skill shows up. It's mechanical, and fine.

beats.trigger: Expect the reusable check to find things you did not think about, and to leave things "I can't tell" you thought were settled.
beats.got: The check should surface things I missed. Where it disagrees with my read, that's useful data.

beats.trigger: Two different lenses; some risks will overlap, some will not.
beats.got: The ranked agent-risk report overlaps partly with the policy report. I then pick one risk to work on.

beats.trigger: The one that bugs you on the second skim. Your gut is data here.
beats.got: I pick one risk by gut, the agent applies a mitigation, and the report states what remains. That's a decision I could show the CFO.

beats.trigger: You must do the work.
beats.got: Nothing new. It's a two-sentence slide that says risk control separates a prototype from production.

beats.trigger: The next agent you build will have a stricter starting line because of this one.
beats.got: The agent writes security rules into the root instructions file, so future sessions behave better. That's something that still works on Monday. The AI-security-is-evolving paragraph repeats itself.

beats.trigger: Give a teammate the skill, install it in their runtime, and they can call the same method without reconstructing your prompt history.
beats.got: A skill is something I can hand to a teammate. That speaks to my fourteen-private-experiments problem, though it doesn't fix shared ownership.

beats.trigger: "I can't tell" is a real answer; closing it takes evidence.
beats.got: It's a recap of things I already got.

beats.trigger: Come to Module 5 without the two missing-check sentences and you'll be reconstructing them while the benchmark is already comparing detectors. Your call.
beats.got: There's homework: one sentence per case on what check was missing. It's mildly pushy.

beats.trigger: what check was missing around the agent's output?
beats.got: I'm to read two cases, the Avianca court filing and the Deloitte Australia report, before the next module, and I'd probably read them.

take_homes: Write the check once as a reusable skill that carries what matters for my own system, rather than rerunning prompts each time. A teammate can load it.
Safe is never certain. I run the loop of assess, mitigate with scope, split, filter, gate or review, then write down the residual and accept it or close the door.
Plain English in a source the agent reads is the attack surface, so my pricing sources need that check too.

monday.move: Run the packaged security-audit skill against the pricing-pilot brief agent and read the residual section. Then drop the skill into the one place my team can share it.
monday.who: Me first, then the two people on my team who touch the pricing working-group brief
monday.when: Monday morning, before the pricing working group
monday.stop_condition: One risk is mitigated, the residual is written down, and I know what I'm accepting.
monday.blocker: My team has no shared place for the context files, so the skill might stay on my machine.

misconception.why: The packaged check, not clever prompts, does the expert work. Writing a better prompt is still part of it, but it's not the point.

one_line: It left me with a security check I can rerun on Monday and the habit of writing down what risk is still left. The generic AI-security paragraphs and the recaps could be cut.
